As far as I'm aware this isn't well studied yet, though I have a few ideas as to why. Style transfer as done in Gatys et al (http://arxiv.org/abs/1508.06576) is based on a style loss that is quite particular to images and the convolutional networks that are used to process them.

The ability of those networks to encode style data is not necessarily an obvious thing--in fact one could imagine that given a different structure and task it would be possible to have an image-processing network that didn't capture style information well at all (I believe this is partly why they use VGG16 instead of a different network in the Gatys paper). Given this, it's difficult to see which lessons to take from style transfer in the visual medium when doing it in a textual domain. There are also fundamental differences in the structure of the data (textual data is sequential and of potentially varying lengths, versus constant-sized images.)

Generating style-transformed sequences will likely look different than how transfer is done on images, and it's plausible we see something like a translation-style machine that takes an encoder reading in a paragraph and a decoder which is trained on a particular author that attempts to read the paragraph out in that author's style or voice. How to train such a thing is potentially difficult though, as such a translational dataset doesn't exist.
